svg.aria-label: Diagram: why VPC Network Peering is not transitive, so a network peered to two others gives those two no connectivity to each other, while the address-overlap constraint IS transitive and forces coordination with networks you cannot reach; why two auto mode networks can never peer because both draw subnets from the same ten-dot-one-twenty-eight slash nine block; what is and is not exchanged, with subnet routes always exchanged and never disableable, static routes carrying network tags never exchangeable at all, and export and import controlled separately by each side; the firewall and DNS boundaries, where rules are not exchanged and network tags and service accounts resolve only inside their own network while a secure tag crosses peering as a source but not as a target; and the documented non-determinism where two peers offering the same most-specific route are resolved by an internal algorithm before priority is considered
svg.title: VPC Network Peering: routing is not transitive but the address constraint is, and two auto mode networks can never peer
svg.text: Peering is not transitive. The address-space constraint it imposes is.
So you must coordinate ranges with networks you have no route to and cannot see.
The asymmetry at the centre of this
ROUTING: net-a peered to net-b, and net-a peered to net-c, gives NO connectivity between
net-b and net-c. Stated outright: peering does not provide transitive routing.
OVERLAP: network-1 peered to network-2, network-2 peered to network-3, 1 and 3 NOT peered
— and you must still COORDINATE WITH network-2’s ADMIN before creating a subnet.
Connectivity stops at one hop. The constraint does not. You inherit a planning dependency
on a network you cannot route to.
Two auto mode networks can never peer — #62, arriving as a hard wall
No subnet range may match, contain, or fit within a range in the peer. And every auto mode
subnet fits inside 10.128.0.0/9 — so two auto mode networks always collide.
A custom mode network CAN peer with an auto mode one, provided it keeps every range out
of that block. Choosing auto mode in #62 quietly decided this, months earlier.
Only routes cross, and only some of them, chosen by both sides
Private IPv4 SUBNET ROUTES are ALWAYS exchanged and cannot be disabled. Everything else
is off by default: IPv6, privately used public IPv4, static and dynamic routes.
Export and import are SEPARATE flags on SEPARATE SIDES. One side exports with
--export-custom-routes, the other imports with --import-custom-routes. Either can revoke.
NEVER exchangeable at all: static routes carrying NETWORK TAGS, and routes whose next hop
is the default internet gateway. Policy-based routes are not supported either.
Firewalls and DNS stop at the boundary — with one exception
Firewall rules and policies are NOT exchanged. Network tags and service accounts resolve
ONLY to instances in the rule’s own network, even if the peer uses the same tag.
THE EXCEPTION: a SECURE TAG as an ingress SOURCE can identify instances in peered
networks. As a TARGET it cannot. So the one identity that crosses, crosses one way.
Internal DNS names do not resolve across peering. Use Cloud DNS peering zones, or authorize
one private zone to every peer — otherwise reach VMs by IP address.
Where two peers compete, priority does not decide
A local route with an identical or more specific destination always wins. But where the local
network has no most-specific route and TWO PEERS offer the same one, Google Cloud picks a
next hop by INTERNAL ALGORITHM.
That selection happens BEFORE ROUTE PRIORITY IS CONSIDERED, and you cannot configure it —
so adding or removing a peer can silently reorder routing. Google says avoid the shape.
Two more boundaries worth knowing: peers may sit in DIFFERENT ORGANIZATIONS, unlike Shared
VPC; and a Cloud Router will NOT advertise received peering subnet routes in default
advertisement mode, so hybrid reachability needs custom advertised mode set deliberately.
Peered networks stay administratively separate. Latency and throughput match a single VPC.
